grammar: 'Regarder' means 'to watch/look at' – the 'at' is built in. No preposition needed: je regarde la télé, not *je regarde à la télé.
'Jouer au' is used for sports (au football), while 'jouer du/de la' is for instruments (du piano). The preposition changes the meaning.
In French, meals take the definite article: 'le dîner' (dinner), 'le déjeuner' (lunch). English drops it; French doesn't.
'Adorer' = to love/adore. Stronger than 'aimer'. With general nouns, use the article: 'adorent le chocolat'.
'Détester' = to hate. With abstract nouns, French requires the article: 'il déteste le bruit' (he hates noise).
'Nous' form of -er verbs: drop -er, add -ons. 'Préparons le petit déjeuner' = we prepare breakfast.
Aimer is a regular -er verb. Use aimer + definite article for general likes: J'aime le café (I like coffee in general).
In French, you 'invite à dîner' (invite to dinner). The preposition 'à' links the action to the event.
'Porter' means both 'to carry' and 'to wear': context determines. 'Portent des lunettes' = they wear glasses.
'Finir de + infinitive' means 'to finish doing something'. This is a common -ir verb construction.
Verbs ending in -ier (étudier) have a double 'i' in the nous/vous forms: nous étudions, vous étudiez.
Arriver is a regular -er verb, but in passé composé it uses être as auxiliary: je suis arrivé(e). At A1, focus on present tense.
'Être en retard' = to be late. French uses the preposition 'en' before 'retard', not 'à' or nothing.
'Venir de' + infinitive = just did something: 'je viens de manger' = I just ate.
Boire (to drink) is irregular: je bois, tu bois, il boit, nous buvons, vous buvez, ils boivent. Note the 'uv' in plural.
Comprendre (to understand) conjugates like prendre: je comprends, tu comprends, il comprend, nous comprenons, ils comprennent.
Apprendre (to learn) conjugates like prendre: j'apprends, tu apprends, il apprend, nous apprenons, ils apprennent.
Conduire (to drive) is irregular: je conduis, tu conduis, il conduit, nous conduisons, vous conduisez, ils conduisent.
'Avoir froid' = to be cold (feeling), 'avoir chaud' = to be hot. French says 'I have cold/heat' not 'I am cold/hot'.
'Avoir besoin de' = to need. Literally 'to have need of': j'ai besoin d'eau (I need water).
For -er verbs ending in -ger (manger), add an extra 'e' before -ons: nous mangeons. This keeps the soft 'g' sound.
'Habiter à' is used with cities: 'habiter à Paris'. For countries, use 'habiter en' (feminine) or 'habiter au' (masculine).
'Écouter' means 'to listen to' – the 'to' is built in. No preposition needed: j'écoute la musique (I listen to music).
Adverbs like 'très' (very) and 'bien' (well) go right after the verb in French: 'il danse très bien', not *il très bien danse.
The 'nous' form of -er verbs always ends in '-ons': chantons, parlons, jouons. It's the most regular pattern in French.
Verbs like acheter change è before silent endings: j'achète, tu achètes, il achète, but nous achetons (no accent change).
'Téléphoner à' requires the preposition 'à' before the person: il téléphone à sa mère. Unlike 'appeler' which takes a direct object.
The 'tu' form of -er verbs always ends in '-es': tu nages, tu parles, tu manges. The final -s is always silent.
French uses 'faire + du/de la' for activities: faire du vélo, faire de la natation. The article depends on the noun's gender.
'Inviter' is regular -er. 'Des amis' uses partitive 'des' = some. French requires this where English omits 'some'.
'-ir' verbs like 'finir' add '-iss-' in plural forms. Think of it as the verb 'growing' when more people are involved.
'Choisir de' + infinitive = to choose to: 'Je choisis de rester' (I choose to stay). The 'de' is required.
'Obéir à' = to obey. Regular -ir verb with -iss- in plural. Requires 'à': 'il obéit à ses parents'.
With '-re' verbs, the il/elle form has no ending: 'il vend' (he sells). The 'd' is the last sound you hear.
'Entendre' = to hear (passive). 'Écouter' = to listen (active). Like English hear vs. listen.
'On' is an informal way to say 'we' in spoken French. It conjugates like il/elle (3rd person singular): on mange, on parle.
Payer can be spelled je paye or je paie – both are correct. Verbs ending in -ayer allow both forms.
'Profiter de' means 'to enjoy/take advantage of'. The 'de' is required: profiter de la vie.
Lever changes the 'e' to 'è' before silent endings: je lève, tu lèves, il lève, but nous levons (no change).
'Entrer dans' = to enter. Requires 'dans': 'vous entrez dans le magasin'. Uses 'être' in passé composé.
Envoyer changes its stem in some forms: j'envoie, tu envoies, il envoie, but nous envoyons. The 'y' becomes 'i' before silent endings.
'Garer' = to park. 'Garer la voiture' = to park the car. Reflexive 'se garer' = to park/find parking.
Verbs ending in -oyer (nettoyer) change 'y' to 'i' before silent endings: je nettoie, but nous nettoyons.
'Toucher' = to touch. Regular -er verb. 'Le mur' = the wall.

target: Vous rendez visite à vos parents.
grammar: 'Rendre visite à' means 'to visit a person'. Don't confuse with 'visiter' which is for places: je visite le musée.
'Partager' = to share/split. Keeps 'e' before -ons: 'nous partageons'. 'L'addition' = the bill.
Interrompre conjugates like rompre: je romps, tu romps, il rompt (with a 't'), nous rompons.
With numbers, no article before the noun: 'deux enfants', not *'deux des enfants'. The number replaces the article.
Pouvoir (can/to be able) is irregular: je peux, tu peux, il peut, nous pouvons, vous pouvez, ils peuvent.
'Pouvoir' + infinitive = can/able to. 'Tu peux venir?' = Can you come? Informal question via intonation.
Vouloir (to want) is irregular: je veux, tu veux, il veut, nous voulons, vous voulez, ils veulent. 'Je voudrais' is more polite.
Prendre (to take) is irregular: je prends, tu prends, il prend, nous prenons, vous prenez, ils prennent. Note double 'n' in plural.
Connaître (to know/be familiar with) is irregular: je connais, tu connais, il connaît, nous connaissons. Use for people/places/things.
Lire (to read) is irregular: je lis, tu lis, il lit, nous lisons, vous lisez, ils lisent.
'Être d'accord' = to agree. French uses 'to be of agreement' rather than a single verb.
Partir (to leave/depart) is irregular: je pars, tu pars, il part, nous partons, vous partez, ils partent.
Tenir (to hold) conjugates like venir: je tiens, tu tiens, il tient, nous tenons, vous tenez, ils tiennent.
Ouvrir (to open) is irregular: j'ouvre, tu ouvres, il ouvre, nous ouvrons. Despite being -ir, it uses -er endings in present.
Vivre (to live) is irregular: je vis, tu vis, il vit, nous vivons, vous vivez, ils vivent. Use for 'to live/be alive'.
'Avoir besoin de' + infinitive = to need to. The 'de' links to the following verb.
'Avoir hâte de' = to look forward to/can't wait. 'J'ai hâte de te voir' = I can't wait to see you.

target: Je parle français tous les jours.
grammar: In French, 'tous les jours' (every day) goes after the verb, unlike English. Present tense for habits, just like English.
In French, 'dans' is used for enclosed spaces: 'dans un bureau' (in an office). Use 'à' for cities and 'en' for countries.
'Demander' means 'to ask for' – no extra preposition needed. 'Vous demandez l'addition' = You ask for the bill.
In French, 'elles' is used for an all-female group. Even one male in the group changes it to 'ils'.
In French, professions after 'être' don't need an article: 'Elle est professeur', not *'Elle est une professeur'.
Voyager is an -er verb ending in -ger. Add 'e' before -ons: nous voyageons, to keep the soft 'g' pronunciation.
'Remplir' = to fill out. Regular -ir with -iss-: 'nous remplissons'. Same pattern as 'finir'.
'Accepter de' + infinitive: to agree to do something. The 'de' links the verb to the following infinitive.
'Nager' = to swim. Like 'partager', keeps 'e' before -ons: 'nous nageons'. 'Dans la piscine' = in the pool.
'Réfléchir à' = to think about. Regular -ir with -iss-. Requires 'à': 'je réfléchis à la question'.
'Essayer de' + infinitive: to try to do something. Note the 'de' before the infinitive.
'Bavarder' = to chat. Regular -er. 'Au café' = at the café ('au' = à+le contraction).

target: Je regarde un film ce soir.

grammar: 'Décider de' + infinitive: to decide to do something. Always use 'de' before the next verb.
In French, age uses 'avoir' (to have): j'ai 20 ans = I am 20 years old. Literally 'I have 20 years'.
'Avoir l'heure' = to have the time. French 'has' the time rather than 'knowing' it.
'Aller à' = to go to. 'Au' = à+le: 'vous allez au marché' = you go to the market.
Savoir (to know a fact/skill) is irregular: je sais, tu sais, il sait, nous savons, vous savez, ils savent.
'Vouloir' + infinitive = to want to. Irregular: je veux, tu veux, il veut, nous voulons, vous voulez, ils veulent.
Devoir (must/to have to) is irregular: je dois, tu dois, il doit, nous devons, vous devez, ils doivent.
'Avoir honte' = to be ashamed. Note: no article before 'honte'. Another avoir expression for a feeling.
'Où' = Where. It can start a question directly: Où est... ? Où sont... ? Où habites-tu ?

target: Où est l'hôpital le plus proche ?

grammar: 'Bienvenue dans' = welcome to. 'Notre' = our (invariable). 'Nouveau' before masculine noun = new.

target: D'accord, je suis disponible demain après-midi.
grammar: 'D'accord' = OK/agreed. Common in conversation. 'Disponible' = available.

english: I'm looking for the train station.
grammar: 'Chercher' means 'to look for' – the 'for' is built in. Say 'je cherche la gare', not *je cherche pour la gare.

target: Nous commençons le travail à neuf heures.
english: We start work at nine o'clock.
grammar: For -er verbs ending in -cer (commencer), add a cedilla before -ons: nous commençons. This keeps the soft 'c' sound.

english: You slow down in the city.
He earns a lot of money.

target: Il passe ses vacances à Nice.
english: He spends his holidays in Nice.

target: Ils emménagent dans un nouvel appartement.
english: They move into a new apartment.
You go back to the office.
We have dinner at eight pm.

target: Ils mangent au restaurant ce soir.
english: They eat at the restaurant tonight.

target: Elle voit ses amis le samedi.
english: She sees her friends on Saturdays.
He knows how to speak English.
We have to do the shopping.
They have to come home early.

target: Il croit tout ce qu'on lui dit.
english: He believes everything he is told.
grammar: 'Croire' = to believe. Irregular: je crois, tu crois, il croit, nous croyons, ils croient.

target: Je dors huit heures par nuit.
english: I sleep eight hours a night.
grammar: Dormir (to sleep) is irregular: je dors, tu dors, il dort, nous dormons, vous dormez, ils dorment. The 'm' only appears in plural.

target: Le magasin ouvre à dix heures.
english: The store opens at ten o'clock.

target: On fait les courses le samedi.
english: We do the shopping on Saturdays.
Do you know how to drive?
You have to get up early.

target: Je mets du sucre dans mon café.
english: I put sugar in my coffee.

grammar: 'Je veux bien' is a polite way to accept an offer. It's softer than 'oui' and means 'yes, gladly' or 'I'd be happy to'.

english: How many children do you have?
Sorry, could you repeat more slowly?

target: Est-ce que tu connais un bon restaurant ?
english: Do you know a good restaurant?
How much is a one-way ticket?

target: L'hôtel est près de la gare.
english: The hotel is near the station.
grammar: 'L'' replaces 'le' or 'la' before words starting with a vowel or silent 'h': l'hôtel, l'école, l'ami.

target: Je bois du café le matin.
english: I drink coffee in the morning.
grammar: 'Du' (de + le) is the masculine partitive article meaning 'some'. Use for uncountable nouns: du café, du lait, du pain.

target: Nous cherchons un hôtel pas cher.
english: We're looking for a cheap hotel.

target: Il quitte le bureau à six heures.
english: He leaves the office at six o'clock.

target: Je rends les livres à la bibliothèque.
english: I return the books to the library.
grammar: 'Rendre' = to return/give back. Regular -re: je rends, tu rends, il rend. 'À la bibliothèque' = to the library.

target: Elles collent les photos dans l'album.
english: They glue the photos in the album.
grammar: 'Coller' = to glue/stick. Regular -er. 'Dans l'album' = in the album.

target: Nous louons une maison pour les vacances.
english: We rent a house for the holidays.

target: J'ai un frère et une sœur.
english: I have a brother and a sister.
grammar: Avoir (to have) is irregular: j'ai, tu as, il/elle a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont. Note: j'ai (not je ai).

target: Tu sais où est la gare ?
english: Do you know where the station is?
Are you going out with your friends?

target: J'offre un cadeau à ma mère.
english: I give a gift to my mother.
grammar: Offrir (to offer/give) conjugates like ouvrir with -er endings: j'offre, tu offres, il offre, nous offrons.

target: Bonjour à tous, comment allez-vous aujourd'hui?
english: Good morning everyone, how are you today?
grammar: French uses 'avoir' (to have) for some states that English uses 'to be': j'ai faim (I'm hungry), j'ai soif (I'm thirsty).

target: Vous prenez le bus ou le métro ?
english: Do you take the bus or the subway?

target: Merci beaucoup pour votre aide précieuse.
english: Thank you very much for your precious help.
grammar: 'Avoir l'habitude de' = to be used to. Literally 'to have the habit of'.

target: Excusez-moi, je cherche la gare centrale.
english: Excuse me, I'm looking for the central station.
grammar: 'Excusez-moi' (formal) / 'excuse-moi' (informal). Hyphen links verb and pronoun in imperative.

target: Combien de frères et sœurs as-tu ?
english: How many brothers and sisters do you have?

target: Bonsoir, le dîner est servi dans le salon.
english: Good evening, dinner is served in the living room.
grammar: Inversion: swap subject and verb and add a hyphen. Vous parlez → Parlez-vous ? This is formal. Add -t- between vowels: A-t-il ?
'Faire' = to do/make. Irregular: je fais, il fait, nous faisons, ils font. Used in many fixed expressions.
Nationality adjectives agree in gender: français/française, anglais/anglaise. They are NOT capitalized in French.
Adjectives with 'nous' and 'vous' forms of être must agree in number: 'nous sommes fatigués' (plural -s).
'Prêt' agrees with the subject: il est prêt, elle est prête, vous êtes prêts/prêtes.
'Content' agrees in gender and number: content/contente/contents/contentes. The final -t is silent in masculine forms.
Faire (to do/make) is irregular: je fais, tu fais, il fait, nous faisons, vous faites, ils font. Used in many expressions.
'Venir de + infinitive' means 'to have just done something': je viens de manger = I just ate.
Croire (to believe/think) is irregular: je crois, tu crois, il croit, nous croyons, vous croyez, ils croient.
'Aller chercher' = to go get/fetch. A common compound with aller + infinitive.
'Avoir soif' = to be thirsty. French uses 'to have thirst', not 'to be thirsty'.
'Avoir chaud' = to be hot (personal feeling). Don't confuse with 'il fait chaud' (the weather is hot).
'Avoir raison' = to be right, 'avoir tort' = to be wrong. French says 'to have reason/wrong'.
'Avoir sommeil' = to be sleepy. Another 'avoir' expression where English uses 'to be'.
'Être en retard' vs 'être en avance' (early). Both use 'en' before the noun.
Être (to be) is highly irregular: je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont. Memorize all forms.
'Aller' is used for health: 'Tu vas bien ?' = Are you doing well? Literally 'You go well?'
Dire (to say/tell) is irregular: je dis, tu dis, il dit, nous disons, vous dites, ils disent. Note the irregular 'vous dites'.
Voir (to see) is irregular: je vois, tu vois, il voit, nous voyons, vous voyez, ils voient. Note the 'oy' in plural forms.
Venir (to come) is irregular: je viens, tu viens, il vient, nous venons, vous venez, ils viennent. 'Venir de' = to come from.
'Mettre' = to put/set. Irregular: je mets, tu mets, il met. 'Mettre la table' = to set the table.
Écrire (to write) is irregular: j'écris, tu écris, il écrit, nous écrivons, vous écrivez, ils écrivent. Note the 'v' in plural.
Sortir (to go out) is irregular like partir: je sors, tu sors, il sort, nous sortons. Don't confuse with 'quitter' (to leave a place).
'Conduire' = to drive. Irregular: je conduis, tu conduis, il conduit. 'Trop vite' = too fast.
Recevoir (to receive) is irregular: je reçois, tu reçois, il reçoit, nous recevons, vous recevez, ils reçoivent. Note the cedilla.

target: Nous recevons des invités ce soir.

grammar: 'Être en train de' + infinitive = to be in the process of doing something. Emphasizes the ongoing nature.
Use 'être' for professions. In French, no article before the profession: Elle est médecin (not 'elle est une médecin').
'Avoir honte de' = to be ashamed of. Yet another 'avoir' expression where English uses 'to be'.
Use 'avoir' for physical features: avoir les cheveux bruns (to have brown hair), avoir les yeux verts (to have green eyes).

target: Est-ce que le magasin est ouvert ?
grammar: 'Ouvert' is the past participle of 'ouvrir'. Used as an adjective: le magasin est ouvert.
'Où se trouve...?' = Where is...located? More formal than 'Où est...?' Both are correct.
'Beau/belle' is one of the BANGS adjectives that go BEFORE the noun: 'une belle maison', not *'une maison belle'.
Aller (to go) is irregular: je vais, tu vas, il/elle va, nous allons, vous allez, ils/elles vont. 'Au' = à + le (contraction).

target: Nous voyons un beau coucher de soleil.

grammar: Mettre (to put/put on) is irregular: je mets, tu mets, il met, nous mettons, vous mettez, ils mettent. Double 't' in plural.
Courir (to run) is irregular: je cours, tu cours, il court, nous courons, vous courez, ils courent. Only one 'r' in present.
Suivre (to follow) is irregular: je suis, tu suis, il suit, nous suivons, vous suivez, ils suivent. Same 'je suis' as être – context decides.

target: Tu suis un cours de yoga.

grammar: 'Chez' means 'to/at the place of'. Use with people: chez le médecin, chez moi (at my place), chez Paul.
'À l'aéroport' uses the contracted 'à l'' before vowels. Full form would be 'à le', but that doesn't exist.
'Être au courant' = to be aware/informed. A common fixed expression.
'Avoir l'habitude de' = to be used to. French 'has the habit of' doing something.

target: Est-ce que vous avez une chambre ?
grammar: 'Est-ce que' is the easiest way to form questions – just add it before a statement. No word order change needed.

target: Pourquoi est-ce que le magasin est fermé ?
Bonne nuit, faites de beaux rêves!
Quel est votre numéro de téléphone ?

grammar: 'Que' becomes 'qu'' before a vowel: 'Qu'est-ce que...', 'Qu'avez-vous...'

english: They have a lot of patience.
grammar: 'Beaucoup de' (much/many) is always followed by 'de', never 'des': beaucoup de patience, beaucoup d'amis.

target: Nous allons en France cet été.
english: We go to France this summer.

target: Ils vont au travail en métro.
english: They go to work by subway.
When do you leave on vacation?
We go away for the weekend.

target: Elle sort du bureau à cinq heures.
english: She leaves the office at five.
grammar: 'Sortir' = to go out/leave. Irregular -ir: je sors, il sort. 'Du' = de+le: 'sort du bureau' = leaves the office.

english: You receive a lot of emails.

target: Nous avons faim après la randonnée.
english: We are hungry after the hike.

target: Tu as tout à fait raison sur ce point.
english: You are absolutely right about that.

target: Ils ont soif après le match.
english: They are thirsty after the game.
What do you want to drink?
grammar: 'Boire' is highly irregular: je bois, tu bois, il boit, nous buvons. Past participle: bu.

english: Do you know how to swim?

target: Où est-ce que je peux acheter un billet ?
english: Where can I buy a ticket?

target: À quelle heure ferme le musée ?
english: What time does the museum close?
grammar: 'À quelle heure...?' = At what time...? Use to ask about schedules: À quelle heure part le train ?

english: How many sugars do you want?
One hour is enough for me.
grammar: 'Il me suffit de' = it suffices for me / is enough for me. Same reverse pattern: il te suffit de, il lui suffit de.

target: Vous faites quoi dans la vie ?
english: What do you do for a living?
What do you think of this restaurant?
Do you have a menu in English?
grammar: 'Avoir' in inversion: 'avez-vous des enfants?' Formal question form. 'Des' = some (partitive).

english: Do you know where the museum is?

target: S'il vous plaît, fermez la porte en sortant.
english: Please, close the door when you leave.
We have been friends for a long time.

grammar: Use 'être' for nationality: je suis français(e), tu es anglais(e). The adjective agrees with the subject's gender.
'Avoir tort' = to be wrong, 'avoir raison' = to be right. French 'has wrong/reason'.
'Avoir de la chance' = to be lucky. Literally 'to have some luck'.
Use 'être' for marital status: je suis marié(e), je suis célibataire, je suis divorcé(e).
'Être d'accord' = to agree. Literally 'to be of agreement'. Very common expression.
'Être en colère' = to be angry. Use 'être' for emotional states: être triste, être content, être en colère.
'Être en forme' = to be in shape/fit. A useful everyday expression.
'Avoir confiance en' = to trust / to have confidence in. Another avoir expression for a feeling.
'C'est loin' uses 'c'est' (it is) for describing distance. Very common in everyday French.

target: Est-ce que nous sommes en retard ?
grammar: In questions, 'est-ce que nous' sounds natural. The inverted form 'sommes-nous' is more formal.
'Gentil' adds an extra -le in feminine: gentil/gentille. The pronunciation changes significantly.
Use 'être' for location: je suis à Paris, il est au bureau, nous sommes ici.
'Être en vacances' = to be on vacation. Note the plural 'vacances' – always plural in French.

target: Elle a mal à la tête.
grammar: 'Avoir mal à' = to have pain in: j'ai mal au dos (my back hurts), j'ai mal aux dents (I have a toothache).
'Avoir mal à' + body part = to hurt: 'j'ai mal au ventre'. The article contracts: à + le = au.
'Être fier de' = to be proud of. The adjective agrees: fier/fière.
'Est-ce que' placed before a statement turns it into a yes/no question. It's the most common question form in spoken French.
'Demain' (tomorrow) is a time marker that doesn't change verb tense in questions – present tense works fine.
'Qu'est-ce que' = what (as object). Literally 'What is it that'. Used for asking about things/actions.

target: Pourquoi est-ce que tu es en retard ?

grammar: 'Quel/quelle' = Which/What. Agrees with the noun: quel (masc.), quelle (fem.), quels (masc. pl.), quelles (fem. pl.).
'Quelle heure est-il ?' is the standard way to ask the time. 'Heure' is feminine, so use 'quelle'.
In inversion with 'il/elle', add -t- between two vowels: 'Parle-t-il ?' The -t- is just for pronunciation.
'De quoi' = What...of/about. Use after verbs that take 'de': avoir besoin de, parler de, avoir envie de.
'De l'' is the partitive before vowels: de l'eau, de l'huile, de l'argent. Same meaning as du/de la: 'some'.

target: Il n'y a pas de pain.
grammar: After negation, 'du/de la/des' become 'de/d'': 'il y a du pain' → 'il n'y a pas de pain'.

target: Je suis fatigué après le travail.
grammar: Use 'être' for states and conditions: je suis fatigué (I am tired), je suis content (I am happy).
'Avoir envie de' = to feel like / to want. J'ai envie d'un café = I feel like having a coffee.
'Être' (to be): je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils sont.
'Avoir de la chance' = to be lucky. French 'has luck' rather than 'being' lucky.
'Avoir hâte de' = to be eager to / can't wait to. Literally 'to have haste to'.

target: Est-ce qu'il y a un parking ?
grammar: 'Est-ce qu'il y a' = Is there / Are there. 'Il y a' means 'there is/are' and is very common.

target: Est-ce que je peux payer par carte ?
grammar: 'Payer par carte' = to pay by card. 'Par' indicates the means of payment.
'Arriver' uses 'être' in passé composé: 'je suis arrivé(e)'. 'En retard' = late. Regular -er in present.
'Combien' = How much / How many. 'Combien ça coûte ?' is essential for shopping and travel.
When inverting with il/elle/on, add '-t-' between two vowels for pronunciation: A-t-il ? Va-t-elle ? Mange-t-on ?

target: Quand est-ce que le train part ?

grammar: 'Lequel/laquelle' = Which one. Agrees with the noun: lequel (m.), laquelle (f.), lesquels (m. pl.), lesquelles (f. pl.).

target: Quand est-ce que le bus arrive ?
Est-ce que tu as des animaux ?
Est-ce que tu as des questions ?

grammar: After negation, 'des' becomes 'd'' before a vowel: 'pas d'amis'. The partitive article disappears.
'Vieux' has special forms: vieux (m. before consonant), vieil (m. before vowel), vieille (f.), vieux (m. pl.), vieilles (f. pl.).

target: Une bouteille d'eau, s'il vous plaît.

english: I am afraid of the dog.
grammar: 'Avoir peur de' = to be afraid of. Another 'avoir' expression where English uses 'to be'.

target: Je suis content de te voir.
english: I am happy to see you.

target: Elle a un appartement à Lyon.
english: She has an apartment in Lyon.
How much do I owe you?

target: Qu'est-ce que tu étudies à l'université ?
english: What do you study at university?

target: À quelle heure tu te lèves ?
english: What time do you get up?

target: Effectivement, c'est une très bonne idée.
english: Indeed, that's a very good idea.

target: Où est-ce que tu veux aller ?
english: Where do you want to go?
How many days are you staying?

target: Les magasins ferment à vingt heures.
english: The stores close at eight pm.
grammar: 'Les magasins' – use 'les' for all/general plural nouns. 'Des' would mean 'some' stores.

target: Un café et un croissant, s'il vous plaît.
english: A coffee and a croissant, please.
grammar: 'Un café et un croissant' – 'un/une' are indefinite articles. Use them when ordering one of something.

target: Une vieille dame lit le journal.
english: An old lady reads the newspaper.
grammar: 'Le/la/les' for general statements: 'J'aime le chocolat' = I like chocolate (in general).

target: Elle veut une glace au chocolat.
english: She wants a chocolate ice cream.
